item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 14: Larger Testing
item.description: How did a Google test end up as an internet mystery on YouTube? In this deep dive on Chapter 14 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Joseph Graves), we explore larger tests: why fidelity is the reason they exist, the gaps unit tests leave (unfaithful doubles, configuration, load, unanticipated behavior, and the "vacuum effect"), why larger tests are slow, flaky, and hard to own, the anatomy of a system under test, record/replay, test data and verification, and a tour of Google's larger tests, from A/B diffs and probers to DiRT disaster drills and chaos engineering, plus how to keep them fast, understandable, and owned. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 13: Test Doubles
item.description: Why did Google's love affair with mocking frameworks turn into a maintenance bill? In this deep dive on Chapter 13 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Andrew Trenk and Dillon Bly), we unpack test doubles: seams and dependency injection, the three techniques of faking, stubbing, and interaction testing, why Google prefers real implementations and classical over mockist testing, the @DoNotMock annotation, how to judge fidelity and when to write a fake, the dangers of overusing stubs, change-detector tests, and why state testing beats interaction testing. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 12: Unit Testing
item.description: Why can a screen full of failing tests contain zero real bugs? In this deep dive on Chapter 12 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Erik Kuefler), we unpack Google's case that unit-test quality is a maintainability problem: brittle versus unchanging tests, the four kinds of code change, testing through public APIs, state over interactions, complete and concise tests, testing behaviors instead of methods, given/when/then structure, behavior-based names, no logic in tests, clear failure messages, and why test code should be DAMP rather than DRY. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 11: Testing Overview
item.description: Why did Google stop trusting smart engineers alone to keep bugs out? In this deep dive on Chapter 11 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Adam Bender), we follow the Google Web Server's turnaround from a mostly-rolled-back release process to a test-every-change culture, then unpack the chapter's toolkit: test size versus scope, hermetic and flaky tests, the 80/15/5 test pyramid and its ice-cream-cone and hourglass antipatterns, the Beyoncé Rule, why code coverage misleads, and how bathroom flyers and a five-level certification ladder changed engineering habits without a leadership mandate. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 9: Code Review
item.description: A two-host deep dive into Chapter 9 of Software Engineering at Google, Code Review, written by Tom Manshreck and Caitlin Sadowski and edited by Lisa Carey. We cover how a review flows at Google, why code is a liability, the three kinds of approval and code ownership, why comprehension matters more than catching bugs, the psychological and knowledge-sharing benefits, best practices like small changes and good descriptions, and the four types of review, plus our take. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 6: Leading at Scale
item.description: A two-host deep dive into Chapter 6 of Software Engineering at Google, Leading at Scale, written by Ben Collins-Sussman and edited by Riona MacNamara. We cover the author's three Always of leadership: Always Be Deciding, with the Web Search latency case and the good, fast, cheap triangle; Always Be Leaving, building a self-driving team that owns problems rather than solutions; and Always Be Scaling, the spiral of success, important versus urgent, learning to drop balls, and protecting your energy, plus our take. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 3: Knowledge Sharing
item.description: How did one early engineer's habit of reviewing every new hire's code grow into a company-wide program? In this deep dive on Chapter 3 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Nina Chen and Mark Barolak), we explore knowledge sharing: the challenges to learning (information islands, single points of failure, parroting, and haunted graveyards), why psychological safety comes first, mentors and the Recurse Center's social rules, asking questions and Chesterton's fence, group chats, mailing lists, and Q&A systems, teaching through office hours, classes, and documentation, respect, peer bonuses, canonical guides and go links, and Google's readability program, including what its research found. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 2: How to Work Well on Teams
item.description: Why would anyone ask a code host to wipe all their history? In this deep dive on Chapter 2 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Brian Fitzpatrick), we open the book's culture section: the Genius Myth and the insecurity behind hiding work, why hiding is harmful (early detection, the bus factor, and pace of progress), the debate over private versus open offices, the three pillars of humility, respect, and trust, and how they play out in practice, from losing the ego and giving better code review feedback to failing fast, blameless postmortems, patience, and openness to influence, plus how Google replaced the vague "Googley" label with an explicit rubric.
